content: For a mild fever, rest and stay hydrated. Monitor your temperature. If the fever persists for more than 3 days or exceeds 103°F (39.4°C), consult a healthcare provider.

Clean the cut with mild soap and water. Apply gentle pressure with a clean cloth to stop bleeding. Cover with a sterile bandage. Seek medical attention if the cut is deep, won't stop bleeding, or shows signs of infection.

Rest in a quiet, dark room and drink water. Over-the-counter pain relievers are generally used for headaches, but you should consult a pharmacist or doctor for personalized advice, especially if you have other health conditions.

Ibuprofen is a common pain reliever. However, specific dosages depend on age, weight, and medical history. Always read the label or consult a doctor or pharmacist for the correct dosage. Do not exceed the maximum daily limit.

Get out of the sun immediately. Take a cool bath or shower. Apply aloe vera or a moisturizing lotion. Drink extra water. If blisters form, do not pop them. See a doctor if you have a fever or severe pain.
Follow the R.I.C.E. method: Rest, Ice, Compression, and Elevation. Avoid putting weight on the injured ankle. If you cannot walk or the pain is severe, seek medical evaluation for possible fractures.

Sit upright and lean forward slightly. Pinch the soft part of your nose for 10-15 minutes without releasing. Breathe through your mouth. Do not tilt your head back. Seek help if bleeding lasts longer than 20 minutes.

Remove the stinger by scraping it sideways with a credit card. Wash the area with soap and water. Apply a cold pack to reduce swelling. Watch for signs of allergic reaction like difficulty breathing or swelling of the face.
Symptoms include chest pain, shortness of breath, pain in the arm/jaw, and nausea. This is a medical emergency. Call emergency services immediately. Do not drive yourself to the hospital.
Remember F.A.S.T.: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services. Immediate medical attention is critical to prevent permanent damage.
If the person cannot cough or speak, perform abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver). If they become unconscious, start CPR. Call emergency services immediately.

Mild reactions may include hives or itching. Severe reactions (anaphylaxis) involve difficulty breathing or swelling of the throat. Use an epinephrine auto-injector if prescribed and call emergency services.
Signs include thirst, dry mouth, and dark urine. Drink water or oral rehydration solutions. In severe cases involving confusion or fainting, seek immediate medical care.
Rest your stomach and stay hydrated with small sips of water or clear broth. Avoid solid foods until vomiting stops. Seek medical help if you see blood in vomit or have a high fever.
For minor burns, run cool (not cold) water over the area for 10-15 minutes. Do not use ice or butter. Cover with a sterile, non-stick bandage. Seek help for large or deep burns.

Symptoms include shakiness, sweating, and confusion. Consume 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrates like juice or glucose tablets. Recheck blood sugar in 15 minutes. If unconscious, do not give food; call emergency services.
Use your rescue inhaler as prescribed. Sit upright and try to stay calm. If symptoms do not improve after using the inhaler, or if breathing becomes difficult, seek emergency medical help.

Stay with the person and keep them safe from injury. Do not put anything in their mouth. Turn them on their side if they are vomiting. Time the seizure. Call emergency services if it lasts longer than 5 minutes.
Do not try to straighten the bone. Immobilize the area with a splint or sling. Apply ice to reduce swelling. Seek immediate medical attention for X-rays and proper setting.
Do not induce vomiting unless instructed by a professional. Call Poison Control or emergency services immediately. Have the container of the substance ready to provide information.
Do not rub the eye. If a chemical is involved, flush with water for 15 minutes. If an object is embedded, do not remove it. Cover both eyes loosely and seek emergency care.
Rinse with warm salt water. Use a cold compress on the outside of the cheek. Avoid very hot or cold foods. See a dentist as soon as possible, especially if there is swelling or fever.
Rest for a short period, but avoid prolonged bed rest. Apply heat or ice. Gentle stretching may help. See a doctor if pain radiates down the leg or is accompanied by numbness.
Apply a warm compress to the ear. Over-the-counter pain relievers may help. Do not put drops in the ear if you suspect a ruptured eardrum. Consult a doctor if pain persists or fever develops.
Gargle with warm salt water. Drink warm liquids like tea with honey. Use a humidifier. See a doctor if you have difficulty breathing or swallowing, or if the sore throat lasts more than a week.
Rest and drink plenty of fluids. Use saline nasal sprays for congestion. There is no cure, but symptoms usually resolve in 7-10 days. See a doctor if symptoms worsen or last longer.
Symptoms include fever, body aches, and fatigue. Stay home to rest and avoid spreading the virus. Antiviral medications may be prescribed by a doctor if caught early.
Avoid spicy or fatty foods. Do not lie down immediately after eating. Elevate your head while sleeping. Consult a doctor if symptoms occur frequently or interfere with daily life.
Increase fiber intake and drink more water. Regular exercise can help. Over-the-counter laxatives are available, but consult a pharmacist before use. See a doctor if accompanied by severe pain.
Stay hydrated with water or oral rehydration solutions. Eat bland foods like bananas, rice, and toast. See a doctor if diarrhea lasts more than 2 days or contains blood.
Keep the area clean and dry. Avoid scratching. Use over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream for itching. See a doctor if the rash spreads rapidly, is painful, or is accompanied by fever.
Do not pop the blister. Cover it with a loose bandage. If it pops, clean the area and apply an antibiotic ointment. See a doctor if signs of infection appear.
Warts are caused by a virus. Over-the-counter treatments are available. Do not pick at them. See a dermatologist if they are painful or spread.
Wash your face gently twice a day. Avoid picking at pimples. Non-prescription creams with benzoyl peroxide may help. Consult a dermatologist for severe or persistent acne.
Use a moisturizer immediately after bathing. Avoid hot showers. Use a humidifier in dry weather. See a doctor if skin cracks or bleeds.
Maintain a regular sleep schedule. Avoid caffeine and screens before bed. Create a relaxing bedtime routine. Consult a doctor if insomnia affects your daily functioning.
Practice relaxation techniques like deep breathing or meditation. Regular exercise and a balanced diet help. Seek professional help if stress becomes overwhelming.
Symptoms include excessive worry and restlessness. Deep breathing exercises can help. Therapy and medication are effective treatments. Consult a mental health professional for diagnosis.
Symptoms include persistent sadness and loss of interest. It is a treatable medical condition. Reach out to a mental health professional or a trusted support person.
Focus on slow, deep breathing. Remind yourself that the feeling will pass. Seek professional help if panic attacks are frequent or interfere with your life.
Often has no symptoms. Regular monitoring is important. Lifestyle changes like reducing salt and exercising help. Follow your doctor's advice regarding medication.
High cholesterol increases heart disease risk. A healthy diet low in saturated fats and regular exercise are key. Medication may be prescribed by a doctor.
A condition causing weak bones. Ensure adequate calcium and Vitamin D intake. Weight-bearing exercises help. Discuss screening with your doctor.
Causes joint pain and stiffness. Gentle exercise and weight management can help. Pain relievers may be recommended by a doctor.
Severe headaches often with nausea and light sensitivity. Rest in a dark room. Prescription medications are available. Consult a neurologist for management.
A sensation of spinning. Move slowly and avoid sudden head movements. See a doctor to determine the underlying cause.
Ringing in the ears. Avoid loud noises. Manage stress. Consult an ENT specialist if it persists.
Can be gradual or sudden. Avoid loud noises. Hearing aids may help. See an audiologist for testing.
Blurred vision or difficulty seeing at night. Regular eye exams are important. See an optometrist or ophthalmologist.
Common symptoms include nausea and fatigue. Prenatal care is essential. Consult an obstetrician for guidance.
Apply heat to the abdomen. Over-the-counter pain relievers may help. See a doctor if pain is severe or unusual.
Symptoms include hot flashes and mood changes. Hormone therapy may be an option. Discuss with your healthcare provider.
Regular screenings are important for men over 50. Symptoms of issues include difficulty urinating. Consult a urologist.
Can be a sign of serious conditions. Seek immediate medical attention if pain is sudden or severe.
Most lumps are not cancer, but all should be checked. Perform regular self-exams. See a doctor for any new changes.
Vaccines prevent serious diseases. Follow the recommended schedule. Discuss any concerns with your pediatrician or doctor.
Used to treat bacterial infections. Take exactly as prescribed. Do not share or save leftover antibiotics.
Use only as directed. Long-term use can have side effects. Consult a doctor for chronic pain management.
A balanced diet usually provides necessary vitamins. Supplements may be needed for deficiencies. Consult a doctor before starting new supplements.
Drink water throughout the day. Needs vary by activity level and climate. Dark urine is a sign of dehydration.
Eat a variety of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean proteins. Limit processed foods and added sugars.
Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week. Include strength training. Consult a doctor before starting a new regimen.
Quitting smoking improves health immediately. Support groups and medications can help. Talk to your doctor about a plan.
Drink in moderation. Excessive alcohol harms the liver and other organs. Seek help if you struggle to control drinking.
Keep a consistent sleep schedule. Make your bedroom dark and quiet. Avoid screens before bed.
Wash hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds. Crucial for preventing the spread of germs.
Brush twice a day and floss daily. Regular dental checkups prevent cavities and gum disease.
Use sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher. Wear protective clothing. Avoid tanning beds. Check skin regularly for changes.
Symptoms include heavy sweating and weakness. Move to a cool place. Sip water. Seek medical help if symptoms worsen.
Symptoms include shivering and confusion. Get to a warm place. Remove wet clothing. Wrap in blankets. Seek emergency care.
Affects extremities like fingers and toes. Do not rub the area. Warm gently in warm water. Seek medical attention.
Symptoms include headache and nausea. Rest and hydrate. Descend to a lower altitude if symptoms persist.
Adjust your schedule gradually. Stay hydrated. Get sunlight at your destination to reset your clock.
Look at the horizon. Avoid reading. Ginger or over-the-counter medications may help.
Check required vaccinations for your destination. Pack a basic first-aid kit. Drink bottled water in areas with unsafe tap water.
Wash the wound thoroughly with soap and water. Apply antibiotic ointment. See a doctor for tetanus shot and rabies risk assessment.
Keep the victim calm and still. Keep the bite below heart level. Do not cut the wound or suck out venom. Call emergency services.
Rinse with vinegar or seawater. Do not use fresh water. Remove tentacles with tweezers. Soak in hot water for pain.
Remove the tick with fine-tipped tweezers. Clean the area. Watch for a bullseye rash or flu-like symptoms. See a doctor if concerned.
Wash skin with soap and water immediately. Apply calamine lotion. Do not scratch. See a doctor if the rash is widespread.
Flush with water for at least 20 minutes. Remove contaminated clothing. Call emergency services or Poison Control.
Do not touch the person if they are still in contact with the source. Turn off power. Call emergency services. Check for breathing.
Rescue the person safely. Check for breathing. Start CPR if necessary. Call emergency services even if they seem fine.
Symptoms include headache and dizziness. Get to fresh air immediately. Call emergency services. Install CO detectors.
Get to fresh air. Coughing and soot in mouth are signs. Seek medical attention for oxygen levels.
Symptoms include headache and confusion. Rest physically and mentally. See a doctor for evaluation. Do not return to sports immediately.
Neck pain after an accident. Use ice and heat. Gentle movement helps. See a doctor for persistent pain.
Both cause pain and swelling. Only an X-ray can confirm a fracture. Treat both with R.I.C.E. and seek medical evaluation.
Joint is out of place. Do not try to push it back. Immobilize and seek emergency care.
Caused by bacteria in soil. Keep vaccinations up to date. Clean wounds thoroughly.
Transmitted by animal bites. Fatal if untreated. Wash wound and seek immediate medical care for post-exposure prophylaxis.
Itchy scalp. Use medicated shampoo. Comb out nits. Wash bedding and clothes.
Intense itching. Caused by mites. Requires prescription cream. Wash all clothing and bedding.
Fungal infection causing a ring-shaped rash. Use antifungal cream. Keep area dry.
Fungal infection between toes. Keep feet dry. Use antifungal powder or cream.
Common fungal infection. Over-the-counter treatments are available. See a doctor if it's your first time or if symptoms persist.
Symptoms include burning during urination. Drink water. See a doctor for antibiotics.
Severe pain in back or side. Drink water. Pain medication may be needed. See a doctor for management.
Pain in upper right abdomen. Often after fatty meals. See a doctor for diagnosis and treatment.
Pain starts near navel and moves to lower right abdomen. Nausea and fever. This is a surgical emergency. Go to the ER.
